meta.audience: The Zoramites of Antionum; God, in Alma's prayer
principles: Trying the virtue of the word
Praying for strength before praying for success

world_behind.title: The worry is strategic before it is spiritual
world_behind.text: Verse 4 says the Nephites feared the Zoramites would open a correspondence with the Lamanites. Antionum sits between Jershon and a wilderness full of Lamanites, and losing it would cost the Nephites.

world_behind.title: Alma chooses preaching over the sword deliberately
world_behind.text: Verse 5 says the word had a more powerful effect on the people's minds than anything else that had happened to them, so he decided to try its virtue. The mission is a policy choice with a stated reason.

world_behind.title: The company is a roster of the book's converts
world_behind.text: Verse 6 lists Ammon, Aaron, Omner, Amulek and Zeezrom. Zeezrom had been the lawyer who cross-examined Amulek in Alma 11; now they travel together.

world_behind.title: Helaman is left behind
world_behind.text: Verse 7 names the eldest son as the one Alma did not take, and takes Shiblon and Corianton instead. Alma 36 through 42 are the charges he later gives all three.

world_behind.title: The Zoramites were dissenters, not strangers
world_behind.text: Verse 8 says they had already had the word preached to them. Their errors are described as things they stopped observing rather than things they never learned.

world_behind.title: They kept a weekly holy day
world_behind.text: Verse 12 has them gathering one day a week, which they called the day of the Lord. Mormon notes it as part of what astonished the missionaries.

world_behind.title: Alma's prayer asks for endurance first
world_behind.text: Verses 30 through 33 ask for strength, comfort, and patience under affliction for himself and his companions. Success appears in verse 34, after all of that.

words.text: Humble petition. The record uses it twice, here and in Enos, where a man cries all day for his own soul. The King James Bible uses it thirty-nine times, heavily in Solomon's temple prayer (1 Kgs. 8). Mormon names it as one of the daily practices the Zoramites abandoned.

Chosen out, selected. The word appears four times in this record, all in the Rameumptom prayer, and once in the King James Bible. The Zoramites use it three times in two verses, of themselves, and once of everyone else being elected to hell.

The stand at the center of the synagogue. Mormon gives the Zoramite word and then translates it: the holy stand. It occurs once in scripture. The record rarely stops for a gloss, and it does so here for a piece of furniture.

Small rings worn as ornaments. The word occurs once in scripture, in Alma's list of what the Zoramites wore: costly apparel, ringlets, bracelets, ornaments of gold. He is describing the congregation as he watches them pray.

Unbelief, faithlessness. The word appears once in scripture. Alma pairs it with wickedness in the question he puts to God about how long this will go on, which names the Zoramite problem as a matter of what they have stopped believing.

Laid on, struck. The record uses it three times and the King James Bible twice. Mosiah 18 has people clapping their hands for joy at the waters of Mormon; here Alma claps his hands upon his companions, and the Holy Spirit fills them.

phrases.term: His heart again began to sicken because of the iniquity of the people
phrases.text: Mormon opens on Alma's body. The word again points back to Alma 8 and Alma 15, and it establishes that the reaction is habitual rather than new. The sorrow in verse 2 is specifically about a separation.

phrases.term: They should try the virtue of the word of God
phrases.text: Alma's reason for the mission, stated as an experiment. Virtue here means power, and the sentence compares the word to the sword and finds the word stronger. The chapter is the test he is proposing.

phrases.term: Neither would they observe the performances of the church, to continue in prayer and supplication to God daily
phrases.text: The specific failure Mormon names. The Zoramites still prayed once a week, elaborately, in public. What they stopped was the daily practice, and verse 23 shows what took its place.

phrases.term: A place built up in the center of their synagogue, a place for standing
phrases.text: The architecture is the doctrine. One person at a time, above every head, at the center of the room. The building was designed so that worship could only happen where everyone could see it.

phrases.term: Thou wast a spirit, and that thou art a spirit, and that thou wilt be a spirit forever
phrases.text: The Zoramite creed on the nature of God, given in three tenses. The insistence rules out a God who takes a body, which is why the same prayer denies that there shall be a Christ.

phrases.term: Thou hast elected us to be thy holy children
phrases.text: The center of their prayer. Election is what they thank God for, and verse 17 completes it: they are chosen to be saved while everyone around them is chosen for wrath. Gratitude is aimed at the exclusion.

phrases.term: Every man did go forth and offer up these same prayers
phrases.text: Identical words from every worshipper, one after another. Mormon notes it twice, in verse 20 and again in verse 22. The prayer is a recitation with no room for anything anyone actually wanted to say.

phrases.term: Never speaking of their God again until they had assembled themselves together again
phrases.text: The line that makes the whole practice legible. Religion happened in one hour a week on one piece of furniture, and the rest of the week was silent. Verse 10 had already named daily prayer as the thing they dropped.

phrases.term: They cry unto thee with their mouths, while they are puffed up
phrases.text: Alma's summary to God of what he has watched. The mouths are working and the hearts are elsewhere, and he lists what the hearts are set on: gold, silver, fine goods, and the ornaments they wore to pray in.

phrases.term: Wilt thou comfort my soul in Christ
phrases.text: Alma asks for comfort twice, once for himself and once for his companions, and both times he names where the comfort is to come from. He is asking for the thing the Zoramites have removed from their creed.

phrases.term: Their souls are precious, and many of them are our brethren
phrases.text: The last thing Alma says before he stops praying. He has spent five verses on their wickedness and ends by calling their souls precious. The request that follows is for power and wisdom to bring them back.

verses.label: v. 15–18
verses.title: What the prayer says about itself
verses.text: Four sentences of Zoramite prayer are preserved and they are built from a very short list of moves. We believe opens five clauses in verses 15 and 16. Thou hast elected us appears twice. We thank thee closes verse 17 and opens verse 18. Nine uses of holy fall inside this chapter, ninth place among the four hundred and one chapters anywhere in scripture that reach for the word at all, and every one of them sits either in the prayer or in the name of the platform it is said from. The prayer's whole content is a claim to be separated, and it says so four times in four verses.

verses.label: v. 26–34
verses.title: The chapter that leans hardest on one verb
verses.text: Wilt stands eleven times in this chapter. Among the one hundred and ninety-nine chapters of the Bible and this volume that use the word at all, no chapter uses it more; 2 Nephi 4 is next with eight. Ten of the eleven are in Alma's prayer, where the petitions run "O Lord, wilt thou" five times over. The eleventh sits in the Zoramite prayer at verse 15, "that thou wilt be a spirit forever." One word carries both prayers, and the difference is that theirs uses it to state what God is and his uses it to ask.

verses.label: v. 28
verses.title: Their prayer, quoted back
verses.text: In the middle of his own prayer Alma repeats theirs: "they cry unto thee and say, We thank thee, O God, for we are a chosen people unto thee, while others shall perish." All three verses in the volume carrying we thank thee are in this chapter: two from the stand, at verses 17 and 18, and this one from Alma. He is not describing their prayer to God. He is performing it in front of God, which is a rhetorical move the record makes no comment on, and the verse before it has just finished listing their jewellery.

verses.label: v. 37
verses.title: A phrase that arrives a hundred years early
verses.text: The chapter closes by reporting what the missionaries did next: they separated, "taking no thought for themselves what they should eat, or what they should drink, or what they should put on." Those words appear in this volume in one other place, 3 Ne. 13:25, where they are spoken by Jesus to the twelve as an instruction. Here they are narration, not command, in an episode dated about seventy-four years before that sermon. The record does not mark the overlap or claim credit for it.

chapter.title: The word is chosen as the stronger instrument
chapter.text: Verse 5 puts the preaching against the sword and says the word had done more. Alma 43 fights a war over this same ground, and the reader has been told which tool was tried first.

chapter.title: The prayer is correct in form and empty in content
chapter.text: The prayer runs from verse 15 to verse 18 and repeats "we believe" six times and "we thank thee" three. It contains no petition, no confession of fault, and no mention of a Christ; verse 16 explicitly denies one, "we do not believe in the tradition of our brethren." Verse 20 then reports the delivery, "every man did go forth and offer up these same prayers," so a form that never varies is recited by the whole population in turn.

chapter.title: Gratitude is pointed at other people's damnation
chapter.text: They thank God that they are elected while everyone around them is elected to wrath. The Pharisee in Luke 18 thanks God on the same grammar.

chapter.title: The building enforces the theology
chapter.text: Verse 13 gives the specifications: a place "in the center of their synagogue," "high above the head," and with a top that "would only admit one person." Verse 14 states what the design requires, that anyone wishing to worship "must go forth and stand upon the top thereof... and cry with a loud voice." Private worship is architecturally impossible. Verse 21 names it, "Rameumptom, which, being interpreted, is the holy stand," and Alma 32:2–3 reports the poor barred from the building "because of the coarseness of their apparel."

chapter.title: The silence between assemblies is the diagnosis
chapter.text: Verse 23 says they never spoke of God until the next meeting. Verse 10 says they had stopped daily prayer. Mormon puts the practice and its absence on either side of the recitation.

chapter.title: Alma prays for strength before he prays for results
chapter.text: Four verses on bearing afflictions, one on success. He asks to be able to stand the work before he asks that the work go well.

chapter.title: He names every companion
chapter.text: Ammon, Aaron, Omner, Amulek, Zeezrom, and his two sons, one at a time in verse 32. The prayer for comfort is itemized rather than general.

chapter.title: The provision is physical
chapter.text: No hunger, no thirst, strength to bear anything. Mormon says plainly that this happened according to Alma's prayer and because he prayed in faith.

applications.title: Try the word first
applications.text: Alma had an army available and reasoned that preaching "had had more powerful effect upon the minds of the people than the sword, or anything else." The decision is stated as a comparison of instruments, and the sword is not ruled out on principle, only ranked second.

applications.title: Take people with you
applications.text: He takes seven named companions and leaves Himni to hold the church at Zarahemla. A difficult errand gets a team and the work at home gets somebody to carry it, and both are decided before he leaves.

applications.title: Look at what the building requires of people
applications.text: One stand, room for one person, high above the head, in the centre. Nobody could worship privately in that room. Ask what the arrangements you take part in make possible and what they quietly rule out.

applications.title: Watch what your gratitude is aimed at
applications.text: The Rameumptom prayer thanks God for election and for others being cast down, "we thank thee that thou hast elected us that we shall be saved, whilst all around us are elected to be cast by thy wrath down to hell." Read back your own thanksgiving and see whether any of it depends on a comparison.

applications.title: Notice a form that never varies
applications.text: "Every man did go forth and offer up these same prayers." A recitation identical in every mouth is worth examining; the sameness in this chapter is the diagnosis rather than the virtue.

applications.title: Check what happens between the meetings
applications.text: The Zoramites returned home and "did speak no more concerning their God until they had again assembled themselves together." The gap between the practice and the week is where the chapter locates the failure.

applications.title: Ask for strength before you ask for results
applications.text: Alma's prayer asks first for comfort and success for himself, then "give unto us strength, that we may bear our afflictions," and only then for the people's souls. The order is his own capacity, then his companions', then the harvest.

applications.title: Do the physical thing at the end of the prayer
applications.text: He clapped his hands upon them and they were filled with the Holy Spirit. The chapter closes the long prayer with a gesture directed at the people who came with him, not at the people he came to convert.

questions.text: What still makes my heart sicken, and have I stopped letting it?
Which daily practice have I quietly dropped while keeping the weekly one?
Where do I only do the right thing when it can be seen?
Have I ever thanked God for not being like someone else?
What do I not talk about between Sundays?
What am I wearing, carrying, or owning that my heart is actually set on?
Whose soul would I have trouble calling precious right now?
